The New Yorker. Founded in 1925 by Harold Ross, it is an influential American magazine of commentary, criticism, fiction, and cartoons. Ross established the magazine with the mission to be not edited for the old lady from Dubuque, targeting educated New York readers instead. The New Yorker became famous for its cartoons, iconic single-panel drawings with brief captions that became a hallmark of American humor. The magazine published debut fiction and journalism from major authors including J.D. Salinger, Roald Dahl, John Cheever, and James Baldwin. The New Yorker became known for meticulous fact-checking and copy-editing practices, with the magazine's rigor becoming an industry standard. It features the distinctive Talk of the Town section, offering witty commentary on New York events and culture. The circulation remained relatively modest at around one million copies compared to mass-market rivals, but its cultural influence vastly exceeded its numbers. The editorial stance emphasized political sophistication and cultural criticism alongside entertainment. The New Yorker exemplified literary journalism and rigorous criticism and launched major twentieth-century writers. Through its distinctive voice and editorial standards, it defined modern American wit and cartoon aesthetics.
